mappings.note: Explains the lunar eclipse and its alignment and the total-against-partial distinction (LO-166), and asks for a diagram (LO-169).
Long morning shadows and short afternoon ones traced to the Sun's apparent climb, itself due to Earth's rotation.
The daily motion of Sun and stars, and the Pole Star's stillness, all attributed to the rotating Earth and the direction of its axis.
Apparent size explains why the Moon can hide the Sun while nearer planets cannot: the outcome traced to size and distance together.
The stem, carrying its own answer, is again the apparent-size question and is mapped on that; the printed answer is the stray phrase day and night and is reported as a defect.
Names the Pole Star as the one that hardly moves, which is the visible consequence of the axis pointing at it.
Names revolution as Earth's motion around the Sun.
Names the orbit as the path of that motion.
About 365 days for one revolution: the period of the motion.
The axial tilt, with the revolution, as the cause of seasons.
June as the month the northern hemisphere leans sunward: season tied to the tilt at a point in the orbit.
December as the opposite case, the same reasoning half a year on.
Names the summer solstice, a point in the yearly cycle.
Names the winter solstice.
Names the equinoxes, when day and night are about equal.
Names the solar eclipse from its alignment.
The Moon can cover the Sun because it is far nearer: the effect traced to distance.
Names the total solar eclipse, the case where the disc is fully hidden.
Names the lunar eclipse from its alignment.
Whether the naked eye may be used on a solar eclipse: a safety judgement for real life.
The Sun appears to go east to west because we ride an eastward-turning Earth: apparent motion traced to real motion.
The stem, again self-answering, is the apparent-motion question and is mapped on that; the printed answer concerns the reddened eclipsed Moon and is reported as a defect.
How a pinhole projector lets an eclipse be watched indirectly: a safe practice described for use.
Shadows swing round through the day because the Sun's apparent position changes: direction traced to its cause.
Jupiter drifting against the stars over months is attributed to both planets' orbital motion: a slow apparent change traced to real motion.
The stem, self-answering, is again the Jupiter question and is mapped on that; the printed answer concerns the safety of watching a lunar eclipse and is reported as a defect.
Explains apparent size through the Sun and Moon looking alike from Earth: appearance traced to size and distance.
Solstice against equinox described as points in the yearly cycle.
Seasons are muted near the equator because the angle and length of sunlight barely change there: the weak effect traced to the geometry.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes twenty seconds, so we see the Sun as it was: a fact about the Sun-Earth system and what follows from it.
The Foucault pendulum as a demonstration that the Earth turns: an experimental proof rather than an explanation from theory.
Star trails in a long exposure are traced to the Earth's rotation during the exposure.
Aryabhata's boat analogy for the westward drift of the stars: a piece of the history of Indian astronomy, so the appreciate-the-story outcome.
Rotation producing both the day and night cycle and the Sun's apparent path, described at length.
Revolution together with the axial tilt producing opposite seasons in the two hemispheres: the full causal account.
